title: Adaptive Delayed-Update Cyclic Algorithm for Variational Inequalities
claim: Our adaptive local Lipschitz estimates are orders of magnitude smaller than global constants and competing methods' estimates, on every dataset tested.
layout: 3 panels in a row, log-scale line plots, shared legend style
description: Three side-by-side log-scale line plots labeled (a) a9a, (b) gisette and (c) SUSY. The y-axis is the Lipschitz constant, and the x-axis is the number of full data passes, scaled by 1e3 or 1e4. Each panel has six curves. Black and green lines at the top are the global constants L and L-hat, and they stay flat. An orange line is the CODER line-search estimate, also nearly flat and a little lower. A purple line is GR's local estimate, which is noisy and moves around. Blue and red curves are ADUCA's two local estimates. They start near the others, then drop by orders of magnitude, with red lowest. A legend box overlays the upper right of each plot. The eye goes first to the red and blue curves falling away from the flat lines at the top.
caption: Comparisons of global Lipschitz constants and local Lipschitz estimates used by different algorithms, on the Support Vector Machine problem with datasets a9a, gisette, and SUSY. See Section [ref] for further details.
abstract: Cyclic block coordinate methods are a fundamental class of first-order algorithms, widely used in practice for their simplicity and strong empirical performance. Yet, their theoretical behavior remains challenging to explain, and setting their step sizes -- beyond classical coordinate descent for minimization -- typically requires careful tuning or line-search machinery. In this work, we develop $\texttt{ADUCA}$ (Adaptive Delayed-Update Cyclic Algorithm), a cyclic algorithm addressing a broad class of Minty variational inequalities with monotone Lipschitz operators. $\texttt{ADUCA}$ is parameter-free: it requires no global or block-wise Lipschitz constants and uses no per-epoch line search, except at initialization. A key feature of the algorithm is using operator information delayed by a full cycle, which makes the algorithm compatible with parallel and distributed implementations, and attractive due to weakened synchronization requirements across blocks. We prove that $\texttt{ADUCA}$ attains (near) optimal global oracle complexity as a function of target error $Îµ>0,$ scaling with $1/Îµ$ for monotone operators, or with $\log^2(1/Îµ)$ for operators that are strongly monotone.
